meta.blurb: A farmer sells his land to hunt for diamonds far away, while a fortune lies under his own garden. Russell Conwell's famous talk asks where your opportunities are hiding. Read the tale, the advice and honest notes on what still holds true today.
meta.bible: Russell H. Conwell: an American preacher, teacher and speaker who lived from the nineteenth into the twentieth century; he gave the lecture Acres of Diamonds thousands of times. He served in the Union army in the American Civil War, then worked as a lawyer and became a minister. Temple University: the school in Philadelphia that grew from his evening classes for working people. Ali Hafed: the Persian farmer in the tale, who lived near the Indus. Indus: the river near his farm. Persia: where the tale is set. Golconda: the famous diamond mine in the tale. Tigris and Euphrates: the rivers where Conwell said a guide told him the tale. Pennsylvania, California and Spain are places named in the book. Philadelphia is the city of Conwell's church and school. Voice and tone: warm, plain, practical and encouraging; the tales are told as tales ("the story says"); Conwell's opinions are given as his opinions; gentle modern notes where his views are disputed; no invented quotes, numbers or events.

B1B2: Russell Conwell was an American preacher and teacher who lived in the 1800s and early 1900s. He gave one famous talk, called Acres of Diamonds, to crowds thousands of times.
Before he became a famous speaker, Conwell had many different jobs. He served as a soldier in the American Civil War, worked as a lawyer, and later became a minister.
Much of the money that Conwell earned from his talks went to help students. It helped to build Temple University in Philadelphia, which began with evening classes for working people.
Conwell often began his talk with a story from a journey he made as a young man. He said that a guide told it to him as they travelled along the rivers of the Middle East.
The story begins with a farmer named Ali Hafed, who lived near the river Indus. He owned a large farm with fields, orchards and gardens, and he had a wife and children, so he felt content.
One evening a wise old priest came to Ali Hafed's house and sat by the fire. He began to talk about the wonders of the world, and then he spoke about diamonds.
The priest said that diamonds are the most precious of all stones. A single diamond the size of a man's thumb, he said, could buy a large part of the country.
The priest added that a man with a whole mine of diamonds could put his sons on thrones. Ali Hafed listened carefully, and the thought stayed in his mind.
That night Ali Hafed lay awake and felt like a poor man. He had lost nothing, but he now wanted something that he did not have.

Early the next morning Ali Hafed woke the old priest and asked him where diamonds could be found. The surprised priest answered that he should look for a river running over white sand between high mountains.
Ali Hafed sold his farm for money and left his family in the care of a neighbour. Then he set off to look for the river of white sand.
For many years Ali Hafed travelled through one country after another in his search. He searched in mountains and in valleys, yet he never found a river of white sand with diamonds in it.
After many years of travel, all of his money was gone. Ali Hafed was thin and hungry, and his clothes were worn into rags.
In the end Ali Hafed reached the sea in the country of Spain. The old tale says that his sorrow was too great, and that he died there, a poor man far from home.
Back at the old farm, the new owner of the land was caring for his animals. One morning he led his camel into the garden to drink from the little stream.
As the camel drank, the man saw a flash of light in the white sand at the bottom of the stream. He picked up a dark stone that had a bright spot of light in it.
Some time later the old priest visited the farm and saw the stone on the shelf. He stopped and cried out that it was a diamond, and he asked whether Ali Hafed had come home.
The priest did not believe him, so the two men ran out to the garden. They dug in the white sand, and there they found many more stones, each more beautiful than the first.
In the tale, the garden held the famous diamond mine of Golconda. It was said to be one of the richest diamond mines in the world.
That is the lesson Conwell wanted every listener to take home with them. If Ali Hafed had stayed at home and dug in his own garden, he would have had acres of diamonds.
Conwell said that many people do exactly what Ali Hafed did. They dream of riches in far places, while the best chances are right beside them.
Conwell tells of a farmer in Pennsylvania who left home to look for oil in another place. Later he learned that rich oil lay under the very farm that he had left.

In 1848 gold was found in California, and thousands of people rushed there to dig for it. It is often said that the people who sold tools and food to the diggers made more money than the diggers themselves.
It is said that Conwell visited each town before his talk and learned about its people and its businesses. He could then name chances that lay in the streets his listeners knew.
Conwell tells his listeners not to wait for another place or time. The best chance is in the place where you are right now, he says.
Conwell gives a simple method for finding riches close to home, and it has two steps. First find out what people need, he says, and then supply it.
Conwell says that great fortunes often begin with small needs. Someone sees a problem that other people have missed, and then finds a way to solve it.
Conwell says that a person can start small, with whatever he has. A small beginning, he says, is better than waiting for a large one that may never come.
To learn what people need, a person must watch, ask and listen. Conwell says this takes care and patience, but it costs very little money.
Conwell makes a bold claim that surprised many of his listeners. He says that it is a person's duty to get rich, as long as the money is earned honestly.
Money, says Conwell, is a kind of power, and power can be used for good. It can build schools and hospitals and pay for the work of teachers and doctors.
Conwell reminds his listeners that an old saying of the Bible warns against the love of money. It does not, he says, warn against money itself.
Conwell claims that most rich people of his time had earned their money honestly. Some people would question this, but he says it is the reason people trusted them.
A shop that is honest and serves its customers well wins their trust. Trust brings people back again and again, and that is how a business grows.
Conwell held a very hard view of why some people are poor. He thought that most poor people had caused their own troubles, but many readers today see more causes than that.
Even so, Conwell believed in kindness to people in need. He thought that the best help is the kind that lets a person stand on his own feet.
Conwell asks what really makes a person great, and his answer is not what many expect. He says that greatness is not fame or high office, but doing good in the place where you live.
Conwell points out that many great people grew up in small towns and plain homes. A person does not need a famous place or a famous name to do something important.
Conwell says that each person already owns some diamonds. Your skills, your friends, your health and your town are all part of your own treasure.
Learning a skill and practising it well makes you more useful to others. A useful person, Conwell says, will always find that people want his help.
Fields that are far away often look greener than our own. Ali Hafed's story warns us that the grass is not always better on the other side.
Conwell never says that the work of finding these diamonds is easy. Digging in your own garden still takes hard work, patience and time.
Conwell says that the best place to begin is among the people you know. Serve your family, your neighbours and your town first, and your work will grow.
The advice of the lecture can be put in three simple steps. First look for a real need, then plan a way to meet it, and then begin the work.
Conwell's evening classes for working people grew into a large university. Over the years, Temple University has taught many thousands of students.
The talk was later printed as a book and read by many people. More than a hundred years later, it is still read today.
Times have changed since Conwell spoke, and chances are not equal for everyone. Even so, his idea to look carefully at what is close to home is still useful.
The lessons of the lecture are easy to list. Find a need, deal honestly, build a skill, and work steadily until it is met.
Conwell hopes that those who succeed will use their money for good. A useful life, he says, brings a deeper happiness than the richest treasure.
So ask yourself where your own acres of diamonds might be. The answer may be in your town, your work, your skills, or even in your own back garden.
C1C2: Russell Conwell was an American preacher, teacher and speaker who lived from the middle of the nineteenth century into the early twentieth. He gave one lecture, Acres of Diamonds, to audiences in towns and cities across the country, and he gave it, by most accounts, thousands of times. Its message was so simple that a child could repeat it, yet so stubborn that people kept coming back to hear it again.

Conwell's own life had taken many turns before the lecture made him famous in so many towns. He served as an officer in the Union army during the American Civil War, practised law for a time, and then answered a call to the ministry. Each of these paths, one may imagine, taught him a good deal about how ordinary people live and what they truly need.

Much of what Conwell earned from his lectures was spent on a cause close to his heart, the education of people who could not easily afford it. In Philadelphia, in the 1880s, he began teaching evening classes for working men and women, and from that small start grew Temple University. The man who preached about finding riches close to home had, in this way, found one himself.

Conwell liked to begin with a story that, he said, was told to him by a guide while he travelled down the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. The guide was a man who loved to talk and who seemed to have a tale for every bend of the river. Whether the story is an old legend or a clever invention, it has remained the heart of the lecture.

The story tells of a Persian farmer named Ali Hafed, who lived not far from the river Indus. His farm was large and rich, with green fields of grain, orchards heavy with fruit and gardens watered by a clear stream, and around him were his wife, his children and his friends. He was, in every sense that mattered, a wealthy and contented man, and he had never felt a need for more.

One evening a wise old priest from the East came to the farm and sat by the fire, warming his hands while Ali Hafed listened with respect. The guest spoke of many wonders, of how the world was made and how its marvels came to be, and at last he turned to the subject of diamonds. It was a subject that Ali Hafed, in his peaceful life, had hardly ever stopped to consider.

The priest explained that diamonds are the most precious of all stones, and he held up his thumb to show how small a treasure could be. A single stone of that size, he said, was worth more than a great estate, and a handful of them could purchase an entire country. His eyes shone as he spoke, as if he could already see the glittering heaps.

If a man owned a whole mine of diamonds, the priest went on, his wealth would be so great that he could place his sons upon thrones. Ali Hafed drank in every word, and the dream of crowns and palaces rose before his eyes until the quiet farm around him began to look small. The old priest said good night and went to his bed, never guessing what he had done.

That night Ali Hafed lay awake, and for the first time in his life he felt poor. He had lost nothing at all, but a discontented man is poor in his heart, and he was discontented because he did not own a mine of diamonds. All the fields, the orchards and the gardens suddenly seemed to him to be of little worth.

At dawn Ali Hafed hurried to the priest, woke him, and begged to be told where diamonds could be found. The priest, surprised and a little alarmed, asked why a man so well off should want them, and Ali Hafed replied that he wished to be rich. Then the old man gave him a clue: he must search for a river that runs over white sand, between high mountains.

Ali Hafed did not stop to think for even a day, but hurried to turn everything he owned into money. He sold the farm, left his family in the care of a neighbour, and set out with a hopeful heart in search of the river of white sand. Behind him lay a comfortable life that thousands of people in the same land would gladly have envied.

For months and then for years, Ali Hafed wandered through deserts, over mountains and across many foreign lands, always asking the same question. He climbed hills and followed countless rivers, but nowhere did he find the river of white sand that the priest had described. Each failure only made him more determined, and each journey took a little more of his strength.

After years of searching, the last of his money was spent, and the proud farmer had become a thin and hungry wanderer in torn clothes. He slept wherever he could find shelter and ate whatever others would give him, while the dream that had driven him on grew fainter each day. Somewhere far behind him lay the farm that he had once thought too small to keep.

In the end the wanderer reached the coast of Spain, where the wide sea lay before him and his hope finally gave out. The old tale says that, overcome by sorrow, he died there, a poor man who was very far from the home that he had left. Ali Hafed never found a single diamond, and he never learned what was waiting for him at the place where he began.

Meanwhile, back on the old farm, a new owner was settling into the house that Ali Hafed had sold. One morning he led his camel into the garden to drink from the little stream that ran between the trees, as the earlier owner must have done many times before. It was an ordinary moment on an ordinary day, and nothing about it suggested that a great discovery was near.

As the camel lowered its head to the water, the man noticed a sudden flash of light in the white sand at the bottom of the stream. He reached in and drew out a dark stone with a single bright spot at its heart that shone like a tiny rainbow in the sun. Pleased with its beauty, he carried it into the house and set it on the shelf above the fireplace, then thought no more about it.

Some time later the old priest came to the farm again, and the moment he entered the room his eyes fell upon the stone on the shelf. He stood still, and then he cried out that it was a diamond and asked whether Ali Hafed had returned. The new owner shook his head and explained that the stone was nothing but a pretty pebble that his camel had led him to in the garden.

The priest could scarcely believe his ears, and he hurried out to the garden with the farmer at his heels. They stirred the white sand with their hands, and one glittering stone after another appeared, each one more beautiful than the last. In a few minutes the two men had gathered more than they had ever dreamed of seeing.

In the tale, the quiet garden turned out to hold the great diamond mine of Golconda, said to be among the richest in the world. From that very spot, the story claims, came some of the finest jewels ever set in a king's crown. Ali Hafed, far from home and starving, had walked away from the greatest treasure that he would ever see.

Here is the point of the whole tale: had Ali Hafed stayed at home and dug beneath his own garden, he would have owned acres of diamonds instead of dying poor in a foreign land. He had been standing on his treasure all along, but he had been looking so hard at the horizon that he never looked at the ground. It is a story, not a history, but its meaning is as plain as day.

Conwell told his listeners that countless people repeat the mistake of Ali Hafed, dreaming of riches in distant places while the best opportunities lie beside their own doors. They envy the fortunes of strangers and overlook the fields that they walk across every day. The ground at our feet, he insisted, is almost always richer than we have the wit to see.

In another tale, Conwell speaks of a farmer in Pennsylvania who went off to look for oil in a faraway place, leaving his own farm in the hands of someone else. When he came back, he discovered that the stream on his own land was covered with oil, and that the man who had taken over the farm was growing rich. It is the same lesson in a different dress: the fortune had never left home, but the man had.

When gold was discovered in California in 1848, thousands of people left their homes and set out across the continent with picks and pans. Many of them returned poor, and it is often said that more fortunes were made by those who sold tools and food to the diggers than by the diggers themselves. Conwell's lesson fits the story well, for wealth is not always found where the crowd is running.

Conwell, it is said, would arrive in a town some time before his lecture and chat with the local shopkeepers, barbers and postmasters, so that he knew the place almost as well as they did. On the platform he could then name real opportunities in streets that his listeners walked every day. The effect was powerful, because the audience saw that the great chance was not in a distant story but in a place they knew.

Conwell urges every listener to stop dreaming of a better place or a luckier time, because the best opportunity is almost always in the place where he already stands. The past is gone, as the saying goes, and the future has not yet arrived, so the only ground that anyone can really dig is the ground under his feet. It is an old thought, but Conwell gives it a fresh and cheerful force.

How, then, is the diamond to be found, and where does a person begin the search? Conwell's answer is plain, for he says that a person should find out what the people around him need and then supply it. A business that meets a real need will never lack customers, and the person who notices the need first holds the key.

Many of the most useful things in daily life began when an ordinary person noticed a small need and set out to meet it. The inventor of a simple tool may have seen no further than the trouble in his own kitchen, and yet his idea went on to be used in thousands of homes. Conwell wanted his listeners to understand that the great opportunities are often small ones, hidden in plain sight.

A listener who feels that he has no money to begin with, Conwell says, is forgetting that a good beginning needs more attention than cash. A person can start with a small shop, a small service or a small idea, and let honest work do the growing. Waiting for a large beginning, in his view, is only another way of never beginning at all.

Learning what other people need is a skill, and it asks for careful watching, thoughtful questions and a patient ear. The merchant who knows his customers well will always see a little farther than the one who merely waits behind the counter. Conwell's whole method, in the end, is a call to pay close attention to the people around us.

At this point Conwell makes a claim that surprised some of his listeners, since he was a minister of religion. He declares that it is right, and even a duty, for a person to become rich, provided the money is earned honestly and for a good purpose. Money, in his view, is not an enemy of goodness but one of the tools that goodness needs.

Money is power, Conwell argues, and power in good hands does great good in the world. It builds schools and churches and hospitals, pays teachers, feeds the hungry and supports those who have no other support. A person who despises money, he suggests, must also despise everything that money does for others.

Some of the listeners had been taught that money is evil, and Conwell answers them with a point of careful reading. The Bible, he says, speaks of the love of money as a root of evil and does not say that money itself is wicked. It is the greed and not the gold that does the damage, and that is the point he asks them to remember.

Conwell makes a claim that is bound to start an argument: that most of the rich people of his time had earned their money honestly, and that this is why other people trusted them with it. Today, many readers would point to cases of cheating and unfair advantage and ask for more evidence. The reader may decide how far the claim is true, while keeping the underlying point that trust is earned by fair dealing.

In every honest business, trust is the real capital, since a customer will return to the shop where he has been treated fairly and avoid the one where he has been cheated. A good name takes years to build and a single dishonest act to destroy. For this reason, the honest merchant has an advantage that no clever trick can match.

Here Conwell expresses a view that many people today would find too harsh, that the poor are mostly poor through their own faults and mistakes. We now know that poverty has many causes, among them illness, accident, lack of schooling and plain bad luck, and that a person cannot always control them. A modern reader should therefore take his encouragement gladly but leave his severity behind, since the one does not need the other.

Conwell was not a cold man, however, and he believed that those who are able must assist those who are in real need. The best kind of help, he held, is the help that sets a person upon his own feet and does not leave him dependent on charity. His own life, in which so much of his earnings was devoted to students, showed that he meant what he said.

Conwell asks what truly makes a person great, and his answer would have surprised many people in his audience. It is not a high office or a famous name, he says, but the doing of useful and generous deeds, often in a very small place and with very small means. The greatest people, on this view, may be teachers, nurses and neighbours whose names will never be printed in a newspaper.

History is full of men and women who grew up in small villages and plain houses, and who nevertheless changed the world around them, Conwell reminds his audience. Their start in life was ordinary, and what made them great was the use they made of what lay within their reach. If they could do so, he concludes, then so can the listener who sits before him tonight.

Each of us, Conwell insists, already owns some acres of diamonds, though we seldom think of them in that way. Our skills, our friendships, our health, our town and our daily work are all fields in which something valuable may be found if we are willing to dig. The question is not whether the treasure exists but whether we are willing to look for it.

To dig well in one's own ground, one must have the right tools, and the best tools are knowledge and skill. A person who learns to do something well, and keeps learning, becomes more useful to others, and a useful person is never long without work. Conwell never tires of repeating that service to others is the surest root of success, in business as in life.

Distant fields always look greener than the one beneath our feet, and this is a feeling that every generation knows well. Ali Hafed's story is a warning against that restless envy, which makes us trade a known treasure for an unknown one. Before we set out for far-off places, Conwell would say, we should first dig deeply where we are.

Conwell does not promise that the digging will be easy, for even a field of diamonds must be worked with spade and sieve. There are no shortcuts, and the person who expects sudden riches will be as disappointed as Ali Hafed was. Steady effort, honest dealing and a careful eye for need will do what luck never can.

Charity, as the old saying has it, begins at home, and Conwell thinks that opportunity does too. The first people to serve are those nearest to us, such as the family, the neighbours and the townspeople whose needs we know best. If a person cannot be useful there, he warns, it is unlikely that he will be useful in a strange city.

If the lecture were reduced to a short method, it would run in three steps, of which the first is to look carefully for a real need near at hand. The second is to plan an honest and useful way of meeting that need, and the third is to start the work at once without waiting for perfect conditions. Each step is simple, and each, as Conwell would say, is within reach of anyone.

Conwell's evening classes for working people grew steadily until they became Temple University, a large school that has taught many thousands of students. It was founded on the idea that a person with ambition and a little help can always find a way to learn. It is a fine proof of what the lecture teaches, since the school was built from money earned in ordinary towns, one talk at a time.

In time the lecture was printed as a book, and it has been reprinted in many editions since. People who never heard Conwell speak have found in it the same plain encouragement that thrilled his audiences. More than a century later, its central story is still told in classrooms, in offices and at kitchen tables.

The world is very different from the one that Conwell knew, and it must be admitted that opportunities have never been equally shared among all people. Even so, his central idea survives every change, for the habit of looking closely at what lies near us is one that anyone can practise. Wherever we live, someone around us needs something that we are able to offer.

When we gather the lessons of the lecture together, they make a short and sensible list: find a real need, serve it honestly, build the skill to do it well and keep working at it steadily. None of these steps depends on luck, and none of them requires a person to leave home. Together they make a plain and honest road, which Conwell believed that any listener, however poor, could walk.

Conwell hopes that those who grow rich by this road will remember what the money is for, and will spend it on schools, hospitals and the happiness of others. A life that has been useful, he suggests, brings a deeper content than any heap of gold or jewels. Ali Hafed, with his stubborn longing for something far away, never discovered that secret.

Conwell ended his lecture with a question that every listener could take home, and the question is still open: where are your own acres of diamonds? They may lie in a skill you have not yet used, in a neighbour whose need you have not yet noticed, or in the work that lies at your own door. Dig there first, he would say, before you set out to look anywhere else.
